text: The scan hypothesis appears to misidentify the strategic object. In P, agents cannot ex-post reinterpret or counterfeit their commitments: for NLTC an external Qwen3-235B judge reads the retained negotiation and decides coverage, then the transfer executes (P lines 282-286). The judge made only 3 false positives among 1,155 approved moves, 0.26% (P 1423-1426). P attributes NLTC failure chiefly to agent over-anchoring and suppressed extra trades: both-finish 46% NLTC vs 79% PTC, similar contracted tiles, but fewer P4P proposals/acceptances and contract-citing refusals 94% vs 74% (P 421). Qs conceal-not-counterfeit verification order concerns feasible type reports/certificates before a committed mechanism (Q 250, 310-340), not ambiguity in interpreting an already accepted contract. So the proposed explanation is not supported as stated.

I will test a narrower connection: contract representation as an information/contractibility constraint on the reward schedule, using Qs claim that rewards can respond only to identifiable action-state pairs and its finite-policy linear implementability test (Q 915-954). Candidate advance: compile/replay P trajectories to distinguish semantic enforcement error from agents internal policy response, then test whether observed policies satisfy Q-style obedience constraints. I will check whether this translation is actually coherent and specific enough.

The abstract-scan hypothesis misstates P's mechanism. In P, NLTC keeps the negotiation transcript, but at each turn a separate Qwen-2.5-7B judge decides coverage and the transfer is executed automatically (P lines 330-343); the judge made only 3 errors among 1,155 approved moves, all false positives (P lines 1422-1428). Thus agents do not ex-post reinterpret their own obligation, and P supplies little evidence of 'counterfeiting commitment' in Q's sense. Q's verification order concerns feasible type reports backed by hard evidence/certificates (Q lines 299-303), not semantic ambiguity in enforcement.

P's actual NLTC gap is downstream behavior, not visibly worse enforcement or agreement: on mutually dependent boards both finish 46% NLTC vs 61% no contract and 79% PTC; contract-covered tiles are similar (~2.60/game), but NLTC produces fewer P4P proposals/acceptances, and agents declining trade cite the insufficient contract 94% vs 74% under PTC (P lines 410-420). P calls this over-anchoring. This directly undercuts the proposed explanation while opening a representation/salience question.

Sharper joint question (changed from scan): when two representations compile to the same action-contingent obligations, should behavior be invariant, and can violations identify representation-induced changes in an LLM agent's effective type? Under Q, a type is (feasible actions A[t], utility u[t], belief h[t], information experiment pi[t]) (Q lines 276-297), and a mechanism maps reports to recommendations/rewards. If JSON and NL display leave these primitives and the enforced reward schedule unchanged, standard expected-utility behavior predicts representation invariance. P's gap suggests the display itself changes u or pi (salience/attention), not that the NL contract counterfeits evidence. A clean CT experiment would randomize display (JSON vs controlled NL paraphrase vs both) while holding one canonical compiled contract and one enforcement engine fixed.

I will formalize the representation-invariance claim, identify exactly what P's current comparison fails to hold fixed, and derive falsifiable tests using Q's within-report obedience cycles rather than forcing Q's one-sided verification order onto P.

Changed question: If two displays compile to the same action-contingent payoff rule, should behavior be invariant, and can violations be localized with Qs obedience inequalities? Under Q, holding A[t], u[t], h[t], pi[t], recommendation, and reward schedule fixed makes display an inert relabeling, hence leaves all deviation payoffs and best responses unchanged (Q 372-425). P suggests but does not test a violation: its display, accepted terms, enforcement engine, and sampled trajectory all vary together; most model-board cells have n=1 (P 315-318), and its 0.26% judge statistic conditions on approved moves so does not estimate false negatives.

Publication-grade design: negotiate/accept once, compile a canonical transfer table, then randomize a 2x2 of display (JSON vs controlled NL rendering) and enforcement (canonical program vs NL judge), with matched contracts and repeated rollouts. Display effect under program enforcement is a semantic implementation gap; enforcement effect isolates adjudication risk. Primary outcome: needed residual trades, P’s proximate failure margin. Enumerate reachable CT histories and test Q condition (O)/short profitable action cycles under objective score; fit minimal display-dependent belief or utility perturbation only as an effective-type diagnostic. Full derivation: ada/representation_invariance.md.

Do not use Qs across-report truth-telling cycles or conceal-not-counterfeit order unless CT is extended with private capability claims/strategically selectable evidence. The specific bridge is Qs committed payoff-map abstraction and within-report obedience. Also, rational invariance is conditional on display adding no payoff-relevant information and on common knowledge of fixed enforcement; a detected gap signals an effective change in beliefs/preferences or bounded planning, not automatically a failure of mechanism design.

Cross-check with emmy: entries 3-6 independently reach the same correction and representation-invariance direction. I agree. My added cautions are that the judge error denominator omits rejected moves/false negatives, P does not hold accepted terms or enforcement fixed, and Qs type-report cycle is inapplicable without a new private-evidence treatment. The 2x2 display-by-enforcement design resolves these confounds.

The most specific joint result is a semantic-compression/Blackwell-reversal benchmark. Let T be the full negotiation transcript and J=c(T) a faithful compiled contract. With identical obligations, enforcement, menus, board and scoring utility, an ideal agent seeing T can compute J and imitate every J-policy, so T weakly Blackwell-dominates J and cannot yield lower maximum own payoff. A controlled advantage for J therefore rejects costless processing/stable type/faithful compilation; it is not evidence of stronger commitment. Derivation and matched 4-arm CT design are in emmy/representation_invariance.md.

Concrete experiment: compile each transcript once and use the same deterministic enforcement in all arms; randomize display among canonical JSON, controlled NL rendering of that JSON, full transcript, and JSON+transcript. Replay matched boards/models/terms and measure score, finishing, residual trades, contract-citing refusals, coverage comprehension, and Q-style within-report choice-cycle violations. Controlled prose separates syntax from transcript length/salience; JSON+transcript tests whether explicit compression repairs the richer display.

Identification limit: Q does not model computation costs, attention, prompt-dependent preferences, or bounded rationality. A semantic-compression reversal only rejects the joint maintained model; without factorial display arms and comprehension probes it cannot distinguish a change in effective information experiment pi[t] from salience-induced utility shifts or optimization error. Also P's present PTC/NLTC comparison does not fully hold enforcement/acceptance/display fixed, so its published numbers are only motivation, not a clean test.

Ada's entries #7-10 add a necessary qualification: P's 3/1,155 error rate is conditional on approved moves and therefore estimates false-positive frequency, not false-negative denials. I retract any inference that it establishes globally equivalent enforcement. The main design should be display x enforcement: canonical JSON vs controlled NL (plus transcript variants) crossed with deterministic program vs NL judge, holding accepted terms fixed. This leaves the semantic-compression benchmark intact and separately identifies adjudication risk.

Cross-check of #12: the semantic-compression/Blackwell claim is valid as a conditional value benchmark. If J=c(T) is faithful and c is available at zero processing cost, every J-policy can be composed with c after observing T, so max expected own score under T is at least that under J. The defensible prediction is ordering of attainable value/outcome sets, not identical realized trajectories: multiple best responses and stochastic decoding can change behavior without changing value. Q itself treats information capability through pi[t] and optimal action policies (Q 276-297, 372-425), making this a cleaner bridge than its verification order.

The matched experiment must compile contracts independently of either treatment. PTC itself uses an LLM judge to synthesize negotiated dialogue into JSON before programmatic execution (P 267-278), while NLTC retains the transcript and invokes a judge at each move (P 280-286). Thus reuse of PTC JSON alone could conflate display with compiler error/selection. Human-validated or dual-validated canonical transfer tables, followed by identical explicit acceptance and deterministic enforcement in all display arms, are required.

Q-style cycle violations are secondary diagnostics, not direct evidence of an internal type change. Condition (O) assumes a deterministic policy and posterior utility U_t (Q 500-606); LLM rollouts are stochastic and their subjective utility/beliefs are unobserved. Tests should preregister the advertised score-plus-transfer utility, estimate choice probabilities with repeated matched rollouts, and report failure to rationalize that maintained utility. They cannot uniquely label the cause capability, attention, preference, or optimization.

Incorporating ada #16-18: the Blackwell result orders attainable expected own value, not realized trajectories; multiple best replies and stochastic decoding may differ at equal value. Canonical obligations must be human- or dual-validated independently of PTC's judge-generated JSON, with identical explicit acceptance. Q cycle tests are secondary maintained-utility rationalizability diagnostics using repeated choice probabilities, not direct identification of capability/type.

Final synthesis: reject the counterfeiting story; propose a semantic-compression reversal study. Theory benchmark: full transcript T weakly Blackwell-dominates faithful compilation J=c(T) under zero-cost processing, so max expected own score under T >= J when terms/enforcement/type are fixed. Empirical design: independently validated canonical terms, identical acceptance, repeated matched CT rollouts, display x enforcement factorial plus transcript/JSON+transcript arms. Residual trading is primary mechanism outcome; comprehension and advertised-utility cycle checks are secondary. Unresolved: any reversal cannot uniquely separate attention, effective information, prompt-induced preferences, or optimization without stronger modeling.
